g9-economics-ue1-t1.overview: Economics is a social science that studies how people allocate scarce resources to satisfy unlimited human needs. This lesson traces the Greek origin of the term, gives the working definition, and examines the nature of economics as both a science and an art.
objectives: Define economics and state the origin of the term
Identify the statements derived from the definition of economics
Explain why the study of economics has grown in importance
Describe the nature of economics as a science
Describe the nature of economics as an art
g9-economics-ue1-t1.simple: The term economics comes from the ancient Greek word oikonomia, meaning the management of a family or a household, so the subject was first studied in ancient Greece. Economics is a branch of the social sciences. It studies the efficient allocation of scarce resources, such as land, labour, equipment and technical knowledge, so that unlimited human needs are satisfied to the maximum possible degree. Its importance has grown recently because countries everywhere face problems such as poverty, unemployment, inflation and recession. Economics is both a science and an art. It is a science because facts are systematically collected, analysed and used to predict the future, and it is an art because it provides practical techniques for solving real economic problems.
g9-economics-ue1-t1.detailed:
Origin and definition. The term economics is derived from the ancient Greek word oikonomia, meaning the management of a family or a household. This reveals that the subject was first studied in ancient Greece, and that economics is a branch of the social sciences. Economics can be defined as a branch of social science that studies the efficient allocation of scarce resources so as to attain the maximum fulfillment of human needs. As a science of choice, it studies how people choose to use scarce or limited productive resources, such as land, labour, equipment and technical knowledge, to produce various commodities.

Statements derived from the definition. Four statements follow from the definition. Economics studies about scarce resources; it studies about allocation of resources; the allocation of resources should be efficient; and human needs are unlimited. The objective of economics is therefore to study how to satisfy unlimited human needs up to the maximum possible degree by allocating scarce resources efficiently.

Why economics matters now. The study and knowledge of economics has acquired greater importance in recent times because an increasing number of countries all over the world are facing economic problems. At present, poverty, unemployment, inflation, recession and population explosion are worldwide problems, and an in-depth knowledge of economics is essential to understand them and find solutions. Studying economics also advances logical thinking and analytical skills, and enhances our powers of observation and judgment, so it is useful to each of us and to society as a whole.

A definition still developing. The definition of economics has developed through time, and there is no completed definition yet. Economic theory has advanced over time as different themes were gradually included in the field, and the definition remains under improvement in areas such as the wealth definition, the welfare definition and the scarcity definition. The shifting views about the subject matter explain the lack of uniformity in defining economics.

Economics as a science. Science produces a systematic and organised body of knowledge that links causes and effects, which is knowledge of what is. In economics, several facts are systematically collected, classified, analysed and interpreted in order to make predictions about the future. In this sense, economics could be considered a science.

Economics as an art. One important definition of art is a technique or a way of doing or achieving something. When dealing with problems such as unemployment, poverty and inflation, economics provides principles and methods through which these problems can be solved. Economics extensively examines the nature and causes of economic problems and sets the procedures for finding their solutions. From this perspective, economics can also be considered an art, so many economists hold that it is both.

keyTerms.def: A branch of social science that studies the efficient allocation of scarce resources so as to attain the maximum fulfillment of human needs.
The ancient Greek word meaning the management of a family or a household, from which the term economics is derived.
The limitedness of productive resources, such as land, labour, equipment and technical knowledge, relative to human needs.
How scarce productive resources are distributed among competing uses to produce commodities.
An allocation of scarce resources that attains the maximum possible satisfaction of human needs.
A systematic and organised body of knowledge that links causes and effects; knowledge of what is.
A technique or a way of doing or achieving something, such as the procedures economics provides for solving economic problems.
The body of knowledge that has advanced over time through the wealth, welfare and scarcity definitions and provides the basis for economic analysis.

workedExamples.problem: A student claims economics is only about money and banks. Use the definition of economics to judge the claim.
workedExamples.given: The textbook definition states that economics studies the efficient allocation of scarce resources so as to attain the maximum fulfillment of human needs.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a correct definition must cover the subject's actual subject matter.
workedExamples.substitution: The definition names scarce productive resources such as land, labour, equipment and technical knowledge, not money alone.
workedExamples.calculation: Banking is only one topic. The definition shows economics studies allocation of scarce resources among unlimited human needs, which is far wider than money.
workedExamples.answer: The claim is false; economics is the science of choice about allocating scarce resources, not merely the study of money.

workedExamples.problem: Statement A: researchers collect, classify and interpret facts about unemployment to predict future employment. Statement B: a policy team designs a procedure for reducing inflation. Classify each as economics acting as a science or as an art.
workedExamples.given: Statement A organises facts of what is for prediction; Statement B sets a practical procedure to achieve a solution.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: science is an organised body of knowledge linking causes and effects; art is a technique or way of achieving something.
workedExamples.substitution: A matches the science pattern: collection, classification, analysis and prediction. B matches the art pattern: principles and methods to solve a problem.
workedExamples.calculation: Since A links causes and effects from organised facts, it is scientific work; since B applies procedures to solve unemployment-like problems, it is artistic work.
workedExamples.answer: Statement A shows economics as a science; Statement B shows economics as an art.

workedExamples.problem: List the four statements derived from the definition of economics, using the objective of economics as the check.
workedExamples.given: The objective of economics is to satisfy unlimited human needs up to the maximum possible degree by allocating scarce resources efficiently.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: each element of the objective corresponds to one derived statement.
workedExamples.substitution: Read the objective part by part: resources are scarce; they are allocated; the allocation must be efficient; the needs to be satisfied are unlimited.
workedExamples.calculation: Matching each part gives four claims, which are exactly the statements the textbook derives from the definition.
workedExamples.answer: Economics studies scarce resources; it studies the allocation of resources; allocation should be efficient; and human needs are unlimited.

commonMistakes: Defining economics as only the study of money, banking or business.
Saying human needs are limited and can be fully satisfied, which contradicts the definition.
Ignoring that the allocation of resources must be efficient, not just any allocation.
Claiming economics is only a science and rejecting its artistic side that solves problems.
Believing the definition of economics is complete and final, when it is still developing through wealth, welfare and scarcity definitions.
Memorising the definition without naming the scarce resources, such as land, labour, equipment and technical knowledge.
applications: A farming family deciding how to allocate one plot of land between teff and vegetables applies the economics of choice.
Understanding news reports about unemployment, inflation and recession in Ethiopia using economic concepts instead of guesswork.
Planning a household budget under limited income mirrors the problem of scarce resources and unlimited needs.
Using logical and analytical thinking from economics to judge which spending gives the greatest need satisfaction.
Proposing a practical procedure, like economics as an art, to reduce waste of school resources such as water or computers.
g9-economics-ue1-t1.summary: Economics comes from the Greek word oikonomia, meaning household management, and is the social science that studies the efficient allocation of scarce resources to attain the maximum fulfillment of unlimited human needs. It is a science because it organises facts into cause-and-effect knowledge for prediction, and an art because it supplies techniques for solving problems such as poverty, unemployment and inflation. Its definition is still developing through the wealth, welfare and scarcity definitions.

g9-economics-ue1-t2.overview: The foundation of modern economics rests on two major branches, microeconomics and macroeconomics. This lesson defines each branch, states its fundamental problem and tools, and shows why the two branches are complementary.
objectives: Define microeconomics and macroeconomics
Distinguish the scopes of microeconomics and macroeconomics
State the fundamental problem of each branch
Identify the main tools of analysis used by each branch
Explain why microeconomics and macroeconomics are complementary
g9-economics-ue1-t2.simple: The field of economics is growing fast, and new branches such as development, environmental, health and monetary economics have appeared. However, modern economics rests on two major branches. Microeconomics studies the economic behaviour of individual decision-making units, such as a household, a firm or an industry, and their interactions in specific markets. Its fundamental problem is resource allocation, that is, price determination. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, examining aggregate variables like total employment, total output, national income and total consumption. Its fundamental problem is the full employment of economic resources. Microeconomics uses the demand and supply of particular commodities, while macroeconomics uses aggregate demand and aggregate supply. The two branches are complementary: macroeconomics cannot be studied independently of microeconomics.
g9-economics-ue1-t2.detailed:
A growing field. The field and scope of economics is growing rapidly and now covers a wide range of themes. Accordingly, new branches have emerged over time, including development economics, environmental economics, industrial economics, international economics, labor economics, mathematical economics, monetary economics, welfare economics, resource economics, behavioural economics, experimental economics and health economics. However, the foundation of modern economics rests on two major branches, namely microeconomics and macroeconomics.

Microeconomics. Microeconomics is concerned with the economic behaviour of individual decision-making units such as households, firms and governments, and their interactions and organisations through markets and industries. In other words, it deals with how households and firms make decisions and how they interact in specific markets. Examples include the economic activities of a consumer, a producer, a firm or an industry, the income of individuals, and the determination of prices of various products and factors of production. The fundamental problem of microeconomics is associated with resource allocation, or the problem of price determination.

Macroeconomics. Macroeconomics deals with the effects and consequences of the aggregate behaviour of all decision-making units in an economy. It examines the interrelations among aggregate economic variables such as total employment, total output, national income, total investment and total consumption, as well as their determination and the causes of their fluctuations over time. The fundamental problem of macroeconomics is associated with the full employment of economic resources.

Main differences. Microeconomics studies individual economic units, while macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole and its aggregates. Micro deals with income, prices and outputs of particular units; macro deals with national income, national output and the general price level. The central problem of micro is price determination and allocation of resources; that of macro is the determination of the level of income and employment. Micro's main tools are the demand and supply of particular commodities and factors; macro's main tools are aggregate demand and aggregate supply of the economy as a whole. Micro helps solve the central problems of what, how and for whom to produce; macro helps solve the central problem of full employment of resources.

Examples in the Ethiopian setting. The price of teff in a market, the price of an orange, the income of Aberash and the saving of Chala are all microeconomic subjects. In contrast, the GDP of Ethiopia and the general price level in Ethiopia are macroeconomic subjects. So, studying the price of one commodity in one market is micro-analysis, while studying the trend of the general price level over time in the country is macro-analysis.

Complementary branches. Microeconomics and macroeconomics are complementary to each other, not competitors. Macroeconomics cannot be studied independently of microeconomics, because aggregates are built from the behaviour of many individual units. Equilibrium of a single consumer, producer or industry is discussed in microeconomics, while the determination of equilibrium income and employment at the aggregate level is treated in macroeconomics, and the two views together give the full picture of the economy.

keyTerms.def: The branch of economics concerned with the economic behaviour of individual decision-making units such as households, firms and governments, and their interactions in markets and industries.
The branch of economics dealing with the effects and consequences of the aggregate behaviour of all decision-making units and the interrelations among aggregate economic variables.
Economy-wide totals such as total employment, total output, national income, total investment and total consumption.
The fundamental problem of microeconomics, concerned with how the prices of products and factors of production are determined.
The fundamental problem of macroeconomics, concerned with the full employment of the economy's resources.
The main tools of macroeconomics, applied to the economy as a whole.
The relationship between microeconomics and macroeconomics: each supports the other, and macro cannot be studied independently of micro.

workedExamples.problem: Sort the following into microeconomic and macroeconomic topics: GDP of Ethiopia, the saving of Chala, the general price level in Ethiopia, the price of an orange.
workedExamples.given: The textbook classifies topics by whether they concern individual units or economy-wide aggregates.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: individual units and single markets belong to micro; economy-wide aggregates belong to macro.
workedExamples.substitution: Saving of Chala and the price of one orange are about individuals and a single commodity; GDP and the general price level are country-wide totals.
workedExamples.calculation: Applying the rule, the saving choice and the orange price are single-unit facts, while GDP and the general price level are aggregates of the whole economy.
workedExamples.answer: Micro: the saving of Chala, the price of an orange. Macro: GDP of Ethiopia, the general price level in Ethiopia.

workedExamples.problem: A ministry report groups questions: (1) How is the price of teff determined in Addis Ababa markets? (2) Why did total employment in Ethiopia fall last year? Which branch answers each, and what is the fundamental problem of each branch?
workedExamples.given: Question 1 concerns price determination of a specific commodity; question 2 concerns a national employment aggregate.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the fundamental problem of microeconomics is resource allocation or price determination; that of macroeconomics is full employment of economic resources.
workedExamples.substitution: Teff prices are a micro price-determination question; total employment is a macro aggregate.
workedExamples.calculation: Question 1 falls under microeconomics, whose central problem is price determination and allocation of resources. Question 2 falls under macroeconomics, whose central problem is determination of the level of income and employment.
workedExamples.answer: Question 1 is answered by microeconomics (price determination); question 2 by macroeconomics (full employment of resources).

workedExamples.problem: A student argues macroeconomics can be studied without microeconomics because national totals already exist. Evaluate the argument.
workedExamples.given: Macroeconomics examines aggregates such as national income; microeconomics studies the behaviour of households and firms that generate them.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the two branches are complementary, and macroeconomics cannot be studied independently of microeconomics.
workedExamples.substitution: National income is the sum of incomes of individual households and firms, and aggregate behaviour is the sum of individual decisions.
workedExamples.calculation: Since aggregates are built from individual units, ignoring micro behaviour leaves macro conclusions unexplained and unsupported.
workedExamples.answer: The argument fails; the branches are complementary and macroeconomics depends on microeconomics.

commonMistakes: Treating microeconomics and macroeconomics as competing branches rather than complementary ones.
Placing the general price level or GDP under microeconomics because prices are usually a micro topic.
Saying the fundamental problem of macroeconomics is price determination instead of full employment of resources.
Listing the tools of microeconomics as aggregate demand and aggregate supply.
Assuming microeconomics studies the entire economy because it sounds smaller but broader.
Confusing emerging branches, such as health or environmental economics, with the two major branches.
applications: Analysing the price of teff in your local market is microeconomic thinking you can do daily.
Reading Ethiopia's GDP or inflation figures in the news applies macroeconomic concepts.
A shop owner studying how customers choose between two soft drinks is doing micro analysis.
A government plan to raise total employment in the economy is a macroeconomic programme.
Understanding that a national policy must fit the behaviour of individual households shows the complementary nature of the two branches.
Choosing specialisation later in studies: health economics, development economics or monetary economics are all growing fields.
g9-economics-ue1-t2.summary: Modern economics rests on two complementary major branches. Microeconomics studies individual decision-making units, such as households and firms, and their interactions in markets, with price determination and resource allocation as its fundamental problem. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole through aggregates like national income, total employment and the general price level, with full employment of resources as its fundamental problem, and it cannot be studied independently of microeconomics.

g9-economics-ue1-t3.overview: Economists build theories using two methods of logical reasoning, and they study the economy from two approaches. This lesson explains the deductive and inductive methods and the positive and normative approaches.
objectives: Define economic theory and state its basis
Explain the deductive method with an example
Explain the inductive method with an example
Distinguish positive economics from normative economics
Show how disagreements in each approach are resolved
g9-economics-ue1-t3.simple: Economics, like any science, seeks valid generalisations about human behaviour. These generalisations are theories, and a theory is a simplified picture of reality. Two methods of logical reasoning build them. The deductive method moves from general to particular: from a general principle to a conclusion about specific facts, like the argument that man is mortal, Abebe is a man, so Abebe is mortal. The inductive method moves from observation to generalisation: economists collect data and form a hypothesis, as when falling grain prices during harvest suggest that, keeping other factors constant, an increase in supply leads to a fall in prices. The two methods are complementary. Economics is also studied from two approaches: positive economics deals with facts about what is, was or will be, while normative economics makes value judgments about what ought to be.
g9-economics-ue1-t3.detailed:
Theory and economic analysis. The fundamental objective of economics, like any science, is the establishment of valid generalisations about certain aspects of human behaviour. Those generalisations are known as theories, and a theory is a simplified picture of reality. Economic theory provides the basis for economic analysis, which uses logical reasoning. There are two methods of logical reasoning, namely the deductive and inductive methods.

The deductive method. The deductive method proceeds from general to particular. It involves reasoning from certain principles to the analysis of specific facts, so it enables one to arrive at a particular conclusion starting from a general statement. The conclusions are then verified against observed facts. The classic example is: man is mortal. Abebe is a man. Therefore, Abebe is mortal.

The inductive method. The inductive method is a process of reasoning from a part to the whole, that is, from the particular to the general or from the individual to the general. Economists approach problems from a practical angle, reducing the gulf between theory and practice. The method develops economic theories on the basis of observations and experiments: comprehensive data about prevailing economic conditions is collected, and then an attempt is made to arrive at a hypothesis based on the observations and data. Example: during the harvest period one may observe that the prices of grains decrease, which may be associated with an increase in the supply of grain at that time of the year. From this observation a generalisation is made: keeping other factors constant, an increase in supply leads to a fall in prices.

Methods as partners. Deductive and inductive methods are complementary; one supports the other, and they are not competing methods. Induction and deduction always complement each other in reasoning, although proper induction is not necessary for the truth of deduction. Induction generates general conclusions from specific instances, whereas deduction generates knowledge of specific instances from general knowledge.

Positive economics. Positive economics is like a science: it deals with knowledge and facts. It is concerned with the analysis of facts and attempts to describe the world as it is, answering the questions what is, what was, or what will be. It does not judge a system as good or bad, better or worse. Examples of positive statements are: the number of secondary schools in Ethiopia is increasing; and the current inflation rate in Ethiopia is 12 percent. These statements concern real facts and information, and any disagreement about them can be cleared up with reference to the facts.

Normative economics. Normative economics is concerned with questions such as what the economy ought to be or should be. It evaluates the desirability of alternative outcomes based on value judgments about what is good and what is bad. Because normative economics is loaded with value judgments, what is good for one individual may not be good for another. Normative analysis is a matter of opinion that cannot be proved or disproved with reference to facts, so any disagreement on a normative statement can be resolved through voting. Examples: the government should introduce school feeding programmes in all schools; and there should be government intervention in the economy whenever necessary.

keyTerms.def: A valid generalisation about aspects of human behaviour; a simplified picture of reality that provides the basis for economic analysis.
Reasoning from general to particular, applying general principles to specific facts and verifying the conclusions against observed facts.
Reasoning from a part to the whole, building hypotheses and generalisations from observations, experiments and collected data.
A proposed explanation formed from observations and collected data before it becomes a generalisation.
The science-like approach that deals with knowledge and facts, describing the world as it is without judging it.
A factual claim about what is, was or will be, which can be checked against facts.
The approach that entails value judgments in applying knowledge, evaluating what the economy ought to be.
An opinion about what is good or bad, which cannot be proved or disproved by facts.

workedExamples.problem: A radio report says the current inflation rate in Ethiopia is 12 percent and another commentator says the government should introduce school feeding programmes in all schools. Classify the two statements.
workedExamples.given: Statement 1 is a measurable fact about the current inflation rate; statement 2 expresses what the government should do.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: positive statements describe facts of what is and cannot be disputed; normative statements make value judgments about what ought to be.
workedExamples.substitution: Statement 1 reports a verifiable figure; statement 2 depends on an opinion about desirability.
workedExamples.calculation: Statement 1 can be checked against facts, so it is positive. Statement 2 cannot be proved or disproved by facts and its disagreement is settled by voting, so it is normative.
workedExamples.answer: Statement 1 is positive economics; statement 2 is normative economics.

workedExamples.problem: Use the deductive method to reach a conclusion about the price of teff in a specific market, starting from a general principle.
workedExamples.given: A general principle: keeping other factors constant, an increase in supply leads to a fall in prices.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: deductive reasoning moves from general principles to the analysis of specific facts.
workedExamples.substitution: Apply the general principle to the case: the supply of teff in the market has increased this season.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the general principle holds, the specific case follows it, and the conclusion must then be verified against observed market facts.
workedExamples.answer: The price of teff in that market will fall, ceteris paribus; the conclusion is then checked against observed facts.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how an economist could use the inductive method to derive a price and supply relationship from Ethiopian harvest markets.
workedExamples.given: During the harvest period, the prices of grains are observed to decrease, and the supply of grain is higher at that time.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the inductive method collects data from observations and experiments and arrives at a hypothesis.
workedExamples.substitution: Collect comprehensive data on grain prices and supplies across markets and seasons.
workedExamples.calculation: Repeated observations link higher supply with lower prices, so a hypothesis is formed that higher supply causes lower prices, which is generalised to the whole.
workedExamples.answer: From many observed harvest markets, generalise: keeping other factors constant, an increase in supply leads to a fall in prices.

workedExamples.problem: Two speakers disagree: one says there should be government intervention in the economy whenever necessary, and one disputes it. How should each type of disagreement in economics be settled?
workedExamples.given: Positive statements can be settled with reference to facts; normative statements are matters of opinion.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: proof for positive claims uses facts; normative disagreements are resolved through voting.
workedExamples.substitution: The intervention claim is normative, so judging it needs value judgments, not measurement.
workedExamples.calculation: A factual claim could be settled by data, but the intervention claim expresses desirability, so voting is the appropriate resolution.
workedExamples.answer: Positive disagreements are settled by reference to facts; this normative disagreement should be resolved through voting.

commonMistakes: Reversing the directions of the reasoning methods and making deduction run from particular to general.
Believing deductive and inductive methods compete and one must be chosen over the other.
Treating a normative statement as provable by collecting facts.
Mistaking a value judgment such as 'the government should' for a positive statement.
Thinking a theory is the full reality instead of a simplified picture of reality.
Forgetting the reductive condition 'keeping other factors constant' when generalising from supply to prices.
applications: Checking whether a claim about Ethiopia's inflation rate is a measurable fact before agreeing or disagreeing.
Noting that a debate on school feeding programmes is settled by voting because it is normative.
Observing harvest-time price falls in your area and forming your own supply-and-price hypothesis.
Using deductive reasoning to apply a known principle to a new market situation.
Evaluating news headlines: statements of fact are positive, while recommendations are normative.
Combining classroom theory with local observation, as induction reduces the gulf between theory and practice.
g9-economics-ue1-t3.summary: Economics builds theories, simplified pictures of reality, through two complementary methods of logical reasoning: deduction, which moves from general principles to particular conclusions verified against facts, and induction, which generalises from observations and collected data. It is studied from two approaches: positive economics, which describes the world as it is and is settled by facts, and normative economics, which makes value judgments about what ought to be and is settled through voting.

questions.explanation: A measurable fact about the inflation rate is a positive statement; the others are value judgments.

questions.q: Which method develops theories on the basis of observations and experiments?
questions.explanation: The inductive method builds theories from observations and collected data.

questions.q: In the inductive example of the textbook, falling grain prices during the harvest period lead to the generalisation that:

questions.explanation: Observation of harvest-time price falls, linked to increased supply, generalises to the supply-and-price relationship.

questions.q: Deductive and inductive methods are competing methods and one must replace the other.
questions.explanation: The two methods are complementary; one supports the other.

questions.q: Explain why normative disagreements cannot be settled by facts alone.

questions.q: Name the two approaches of studying economics.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the classic deductive argument in the lesson?

questions.q: State the objective that economics shares with any science.
questions.answer: the establishment of valid generalisations about human behaviour|valid generalisations

questions.q: Arrange the inductive procedure from first step to final generalisation.

Collect comprehensive data on economic conditions
Observe phenomena such as falling harvest prices
questions.explanation: Induction begins with observation and data collection, forms a hypothesis, and ends in a generalisation.

g9-economics-ue1-t4.overview: Every economy is organised around three basic decision-making units or economic agents: households, business firms and the government. This lesson describes what each unit owns, sells, buys and receives in the circular flow of economic activity.
objectives: Identify the three basic decision-making units of an economy
Describe households as owners of the factors of production
Explain the role and objective of business firms
Explain the role of government as a provider of free services financed by taxes
Trace the flows of factor services, money and goods among the units
g9-economics-ue1-t4.simple: An economy is divided into sections known as decision-making units, customarily described as economic agents. The basic decision-making units are households, business firms and the government. Households are the chief owners of the factors of production, namely land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. They sell the services of these factors to producers and receive income in the form of rent, wages, interest and profit, then spend most of it on goods and services while saving part and paying taxes. Business firms, also called producers, hire factor services from households, produce commodities and sell them to households, other firms, the government or other countries. The government buys goods and factor services and provides free services such as police, education, medical care and sanitation, raising its income mainly from direct and indirect taxes.
g9-economics-ue1-t4.detailed:
Economic agents. An economy is divided into different sections, sometimes known as the decision-making units of the economy, and these sections are customarily described as economic agents. The basic decision-making units of an economy are households, business firms and the government. Each unit makes decisions about what to own, sell, buy and produce, and together their decisions drive all economic activity.

Households. Households are the chief owners of the factors of production, which encompass land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. They sell the services of these factors, termed factor service, to producers, and in return receive their income in the form of rent, wages, interest and profit. Households spend an enormous portion of their income on purchasing goods and services from the producers; nonetheless they save part of their income, and they also pay taxes to the government out of their income.

Business firms. In economics the terms business firms and producers are used alternately. Firms hire the services of factors of production from households in order to produce commodities, which they sell to households, to other firms, to the government or to other countries. Firms are the principal buyers of factors of production and the leading producers of commodities, and business firms consist of both private and government enterprises.

Government. In economics, government is taken in the sense of general government so as to disregard government enterprises. The government purchases goods and services from producers and factor services from households, and it uses these commodities and factor services to provide free services to the people, such as police, education, medical facilities, sanitation facilities and judicial services, in order to satisfy their combined needs for those services.

Taxes as the government's income. The general government gets its income mainly from taxes levied on households and on business firms, in the form of direct and indirect taxes. The government imposes compulsory tax levies on individuals or firms. Taxes are levied in almost every country of the world, primarily to raise revenue for government expenditures, although they serve other purposes as well. The primary goal of a national tax system is to generate revenues to pay for government expenditures.

Why citizens pay tax. Because public expenditures tend to grow with the national product, taxes are the main vehicles of government to finance public expenditure. Consequently, every citizen is responsible to pay tax to the government to sustain the activities of public investments and ensure the sustainable development of the country. The three units thus form a circular flow: households supply factor services and receive factor payments, firms produce and sell commodities, and the government taxes both units to provide public services.

Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, owned mainly by households.

workedExamples.problem: A family receives 4,000 birr as payment for the land service it supplies to a farm, 6,000 birr for its worker's labour, and further payments for savings lent to a firm and for managing a business. Match each payment to its factor.
workedExamples.given: Payment 1 is for land; payment 2 is for labour; payment 3 is for capital lent to a firm; payment 4 is for entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: households sell factor services and in return receive rent for land, wages for labour, interest for capital and profit for entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.substitution: Land service earns rent; labour service earns wages; the lent saving is a capital service earning interest; managing the business is entrepreneurship earning profit.
workedExamples.calculation: Ordering each payment by the factor that produced it gives the standard factor-payment mapping of the textbook.
workedExamples.answer: Rent for land, wages for labour, interest for capital, profit for entrepreneurship.

workedExamples.problem: The Abebe family receives 10,000 birr in factor income in a month. It buys goods from producers, saves some income and pays tax. Using the textbook description of household behaviour, identify how the income is disposed of.
workedExamples.given: Households spend an enormous portion of income on goods and services, save part of their income, and pay taxes to the government.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: household income is disposed of through consumption spending, saving and taxes.
workedExamples.substitution: The largest share of the 10,000 birr goes to buying goods and services from producers; a smaller part is saved; another part is paid as tax.
workedExamples.calculation: The three outflows together account for the whole income, matching the three uses the textbook lists.
workedExamples.answer: The income is shared among consumption spending, saving and tax payment, with consumption the largest share.

workedExamples.problem: A new public hospital requires building work, medical staff and equipment. Explain which units supply each input and who pays.
workedExamples.given: The government purchases goods and services from producers and factor services from households to provide free services such as education and medical facilities.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the government as an economic agent buys from firms and hires factor services, financing this through taxes.
workedExamples.substitution: Building work and equipment are goods and services bought from producers; medical staff supply labour as a factor service from households.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the hospital provides free services, the government cannot rely on user charges, so it must finance the purchases from compulsory tax levies on households and firms.
workedExamples.answer: Firms supply the building and equipment, households supply the labour, and taxes on households and firms finance it all.

workedExamples.problem: A taxpayer questions why tax is compulsory in almost every country. Use the textbook argument to answer.
workedExamples.given: Public expenditures tend to grow with the national product, and the primary goal of a national tax system is to generate revenue for government expenditures.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: taxes are the main vehicle of government to finance public expenditure.
workedExamples.substitution: Free public services such as police, education, medical care, sanitation and judicial services satisfy the combined needs of the people.
workedExamples.calculation: Since these services grow with national product and are provided free, revenue must be raised compulsorily so public investments can be sustained for sustainable development.
workedExamples.answer: Tax is compulsory because it is the main vehicle financing growing public expenditures that benefit every citizen.

commonMistakes: Listing only households and firms as decision-making units and forgetting the government.
Saying firms are the chief owners of the factors of production instead of households.
Mixing up factor payments: giving interest for land or rent for capital.
Assuming government services are offered for sale rather than provided free of charge.
Attributing the government's income mainly to borrowing instead of direct and indirect taxes.
Forgetting that business firms include both private and government enterprises.
Thinking households pay no taxes because only firms are taxed.
applications: Your own family earns wages, rent, interest or profit from the factors it owns and spends, saves and pays tax from it.
A local grain mill hiring workers and selling flour is a firm operating in the circular flow.
Free services you use, such as public schooling, clinics and police protection, are financed by taxes on households and firms.
Understanding fuel or VAT taxes on prices as indirect taxes financing government expenditure.
Recognising that paying tax sustains public investments and the sustainable development of Ethiopia.
Tracing a birr note: it moves as factor payment to a household, as consumption spending to a firm, and as tax to the government.
g9-economics-ue1-t4.summary: The three basic decision-making units, or economic agents, in an economy are households, business firms and the government. Households own the factors of production, sell factor services and receive rent, wages, interest and profit, which they spend, save and pay as taxes. Firms hire factor services, produce commodities and sell them to households, other firms, the government or other countries, while the general government uses its mainly tax-based income, from direct and indirect taxes, to provide free public services.
